title: The Covenant Test: Why Stocking Up for Christmas Can Quietly Breach a Loan Agreement
linkedin:
Christmas stock gets paid for in October and November. The sales that justify it don't land until December, sometimes January.

Here's where that creates a problem most owners never see coming. If your banking facility carries a leverage covenant, tested against trailing twelve month EBITDA, the debt you draw down for Christmas stock shows up in that number immediately. The EBITDA from actually selling that stock doesn't show up until weeks later.

Depending on the test date written into the facility letter, a business can look temporarily worse geared than it has all year, in the exact month it's about to post its best result.

We see this more often in confident, well-run businesses than struggling ones, because it's the confident ones drawing down extra funding ahead of a peak trading period.

Nobody at the bank is trying to catch anyone out. Covenant testing is mechanical. A relationship manager working off a trailing twelve month spreadsheet has no visibility into the strong weeks about to land in your accounts.

The fix isn't complicated. Know your test date. Model where the ratio sits on that date given what's already been drawn down. If headroom is tight, raise it with the lender before the test, forecast attached, rather than after a breach notice lands mid trading peak.

For East Coast business owners who have drawn on an overdraft, equipment loan or increased facility to fund Christmas stock or extra trading capacity, there is a timing detail worth checking before the busiest weeks of the year arrive.

Most bank facilities carry a covenant, often a leverage ratio comparing total debt to earnings, tested at a fixed date against trailing twelve month figures. Debt drawn to fund Christmas stock shows up in that calculation immediately. The sales and margin that stock generates do not show up until the trading result is actually reported, which can be weeks or months later depending on the test date.

This means a business that is genuinely trading well can show up temporarily outside its covenant, purely because of when the test falls relative to when the stock sells. Lenders are not trying to catch anyone out here. It is a mechanical calculation, and the business is usually the only party that can see the stronger weeks already on the way.

The businesses that avoid an awkward conversation with the bank are the ones who check their test date and model the numbers before drawing down further funding, not after.
